questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.name: Edit
schema.description:

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': absolute path (no ~) to the built .app bundle (e.g. /Users/me/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/MyApp-abc123/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

text.description: For 'text': the string to type.

name.description: For 'button': hardware button to press.

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

content.content:
<#
.SYNOPSIS
    Builds, validates, and imports the local Maester module.

.DESCRIPTION
    Creates the publishable module under ./module, validates the build output,
    unloads any currently loaded Maester module, and imports the local build into
    the caller's global session so it remains available after this script exits.
    When BuildReport is specified, also builds the report web app and copies its
    generated HTML into the PowerShell assets before building the module.

.PARAMETER BuildReport
    Runs the report npm build and copies report/dist/index.html to
    powershell/assets/ReportTemplate.html before building the local module.
    Report dependencies must already be installed.

.EXAMPLE
    ./build/Build-LocalMaester.ps1

    Builds and imports the local Maester module. Invoke-Maester then runs the built-in tests from
    the module; pass -Path to also run custom tests.

.EXAMPLE
    ./build/Build-LocalMaester.ps1 -BuildReport

    Builds and embeds the report template, then builds, validates, and imports
    the local Maester module.
#>
[Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.SuppressMessageAttribute('PSAvoidUsingWriteHost', '', Justification = 'Developer helper that reports the imported module path.')]
[CmdletBinding()]
param (
    [Parameter()]
    [switch] $BuildReport
)

Set-StrictMode -Version Latest
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'

$BuildScript = Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'Build-MaesterModule.ps1'
$ValidationScript = Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'Test-MaesterModuleOutput.ps1'
$ModulePath = Join-Path $PSScriptRoot '../module'
$ModuleManifestPath = Join-Path $ModulePath 'Maester.psd1'
$ReportProjectPath = Join-Path $PSScriptRoot '../report'
$ReportOutputPath = Join-Path $ReportProjectPath 'dist/index.html'
$ReportTemplatePath = Join-Path $PSScriptRoot '../powershell/assets/ReportTemplate.html'
$ProgressActivity = 'Preparing local Maester module'

try {
    if ($BuildReport.IsPresent) {
        Write-Progress -Activity $ProgressActivity -Status 'Building report' -PercentComplete 5

        $NpmCommand = Get-Command -Name 'npm' -CommandType Application -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
            Select-Object -First 1
        if (-not $NpmCommand) {
            throw 'npm is required to build the report but was not found.'
        }

        & $NpmCommand.Source --prefix $ReportProjectPath run build
        $NpmExitCode = $LASTEXITCODE
        if ($NpmExitCode -ne 0) {
            throw "Report build failed with npm exit code $NpmExitCode."
        }
        if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $ReportOutputPath -PathType Leaf)) {
            throw "Report build did not produce the expected file: '$ReportOutputPath'."
        }

        Write-Progress -Activity $ProgressActivity -Status 'Copying report template' -PercentComplete 25
        Copy-Item -LiteralPath $ReportOutputPath -Destination $ReportTemplatePath -Force
    }

    $ModuleBuildProgress = if ($BuildReport.IsPresent) { 35 } else { 10 }
    Write-Progress -Activity $ProgressActivity -Status 'Building module' -PercentComplete $ModuleBuildProgress

    Get-Module -Name Maester -All | Remove-Module -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
    & $BuildScript 1>$null 3>$null 4>$null 5>$null 6>$null

    Write-Progress -Activity $ProgressActivity -Status 'Validating build' -PercentComplete 70
    & $ValidationScript -ModulePath $ModulePath 1>$null 3>$null 4>$null 5>$null 6>$null

    Write-Progress -Activity $ProgressActivity -Status 'Loading local module' -PercentComplete 90

content.text:
You can run it two ways. Both use the worktree, because none of this is on `main` yet.

## Quick look: the report dev server

This doesn't need a tenant. It loads the sample results and builds the plan from the pack's workshop files, the same way the pack does at run time.

```bash
cd /Users/merill/github/maester/.claude/worktrees/zero-trust-view/report
```

```bash
npm ci
```

```bash
npm run dev -- --port 5174
```

Then open http://localhost:5174/#/zero-trust, or click **Zero Trust plan** under Packs in the sidebar. Port 5173 is your main checkout's report server, which is why this uses 5174.

## Full run against your tenant

From a PowerShell 7.4+ session:

```bash
cd /Users/merill/github/maester/.claude/worktrees/zero-trust-view
```

```bash
pwsh -NoExit -Command "./build/Build-LocalMaester.ps1 -BuildReport"
```

`-BuildReport` builds the React report and copies it into `powershell/assets/ReportTemplate.html`. It then builds the module and imports it into your session. Next, in that same session:

```powershell
Install-Module ZeroTrustAssessment -Scope CurrentUser   # once
Connect-Maester
Invoke-Maester -Pack ZTA -SkipBuiltIn   # or drop -SkipBuiltIn to include Maester's tests
```

Open the generated report and choose **Zero Trust plan**. This run also covers `ZeroTrustAssessmentPack.Tests.ps1`, which I haven't run: it checks that the plan is attached.

**Note:** the build overwrites `ReportTemplate.html`. Don't commit it, because CI builds that file. Afterwards, put it back with:

```bash
git checkout -- powershell/assets/ReportTemplate.html
```

content.text:
I swapped it out myself, and I should have asked you first. I mentioned it only in passing, in the summary at the end.

In prototype G, Cytoscape only drew the diagram. The prototype's own code already worked out where each box went (a "preset" layout of swimlanes by phases). I rebuilt the drawing as plain HTML boxes with an SVG layer for the arrows, on a canvas you can pan and zoom. The layout logic is the same. Here's why I swapped it:

- **Report size.** The report is one self-contained HTML file, so every library is inlined into every report, whether or not the ZTA pack ran. Cytoscape's minified build is about 430 KB, which would roughly double the report template (currently 477 KB). The HTML version adds about 50 KB in total, styles included.
- **It fits the rest of the report.** The boxes are real buttons that use the report's own styles and colour variables. Dark mode, the status colours, keyboard focus and screen-reader labels work the way they do everywhere else in the report. Cytoscape draws onto a canvas, so all of that would have to be rebuilt separately.
- **Scrolling.** The bug you reported was Cytoscape taking every scroll on the diagram. Handling the scroll wheel myself made it easy to let a plain scroll move the page and use Ctrl/⌘ + scroll to zoom.

What you'd lose compared with G: Cytoscape's smooth canvas rendering at very low zoom levels, and its built-in animated panning. The text on the boxes is also small when the whole diagram is fitted to the width.

If you'd rather have G's diagram exactly as it was, I can switch it back to Cytoscape. The rest of the view, including the layout code and the flyover, stays the same either way. The cost is about 430 KB on every report.

used, because Maester cannot redact the assessment's report.

## Zero Trust plan

The report's **Zero Trust plan** view shows the [Microsoft Zero Trust Workshop](https://zerotrust.microsoft.com)
plan for the tenant. Each pillar (Identity, Devices, Data, Network, Infrastructure, Security Operations and AI) is
split into functional areas and swimlanes, and each task has its phase, priority, effort, user impact, licence,
dependencies and Microsoft's guidance. A task shows the status of the checks that measure it, so you can see which
parts of the plan are done, which fail and which no check covers yet. The pillars the run has results for are marked.

A task's checks come from three places:

- the assessment tests Microsoft maps to the task;
- Maester's built-in tests that check the same setting as one of those assessment tests;
- Maester tests that Maester maps to the task itself, with a note where it checks more than the workshop asks.

Maester also adds a few tasks the workshop does not have, such as hardening Microsoft Entra Connect sync. They are
marked as Maester's. Run Maester's own tests with the pack (`Invoke-Maester -Pack ZTA`) to see their status.

The plan ships with the pack, so the view works offline. Set `ZeroTrustAssessment.WorkshopPlan` to `false` to
leave it out. With `Invoke-Maester -RedactUserIdentity` the plan is kept, redacted like the results.

The custom diagram is gone. The Zero Trust plan now opens on Option A's swimlane board, and the table is the second view.

**Swimlanes (default, `#/zero-trust/<pillar>`):**
- **Area picker:** cards for the functional areas, each with its progress bar. It starts on the area of the first "Do these next" task.
- **Board:** below the cards, the board for the chosen area. Its swimlanes are rows and First / Then / Next are columns. The current phase's column is tinted and marked "You are here".
- **Cards:** each task is a card with its icon, a status-coloured edge, "N of M checks pass", its priority and "after X" when something has to come first. Tasks you review yourself have dashed outlines.
- **Header:** the phase header stays visible under the top bar as you scroll.
- **Filters:** search and the filters hide tasks that don't match, the same as in the table.
- **Narrow screens:** on a phone, or in a narrow window, each lane's phases stack under the lane name, as in A.

**Table (`#/zero-trust/<pillar>/table`):** unchanged. The "Diagram" link on each area row is now "Swimlanes".

**Moving between views:**
- Clicking a card opens the same right-hand flyover as before.
- The flyover's button reads "Show in the table" or "Show in the swimlanes". It switches views and scrolls to that task.
- "Do these next" switches to the task's area and scrolls the card to the middle of the screen.

The diagram component and its layout code are deleted. The pack docs now describe the two views.

I checked it on the dev server: desktop and phone width, dark mode, switching views both ways, and every "Do these next" link. There were no console errors and no sideways scrolling on a phone. The report builds at 523 KB, about 7 KB smaller than with the diagram.

To try it, the dev server is running at http://localhost:5175/#/zero-trust. Port 5174 was taken, so it moved to 5175.

files.content: @AGENTS.md

# AGENTS.md

Maester is a PowerShell framework for monitoring Microsoft 365 security
configuration, with its own test engine. Pester is used only for the module's unit tests
and to run users' Pester-format custom tests. Requires PowerShell 7.4+. Monorepo: `powershell/` (module source),
`tests/` (security checks shipped to users), `src/Maester.Engine/` (C# engine core,
built DLL committed in `powershell/lib/`), `build/`, `website/` (Astro + Starlight,
maester.dev), `report/` (React app that builds the HTML report template).

## Two unrelated test trees — don't mix them

- `tests/` — Maester **security checks** that ship to end-user tenants, run via
  `Invoke-Maester`. Each check is a native test: `tests/<suite>/[<service>/]Test.<ID>.ps1`
  (one function with a `[MaesterTest(...)]` attribute) plus `Test.<ID>.md`. No
  `*.Tests.ps1` wrappers, no connection/licence guards, no outer try/catch: declare
  `Service`/`License` and the engine handles them. Scaffold with `New-MtTest`,
  validate with `Get-MtTest <ID>` (`Get-MtTest -Path` applies the rules of a custom test
  and does not report a missing attribute), run with `Invoke-MtTest -Path`; `Convert-MtTest`
  converts users' Pester-format tests. New MT.xxxx checks go here; follow
  `.github/skills/maester-test-expert/SKILL.md` and `website/docs/writing-tests/index.mdx`,
  and choose the attribute values with `website/docs/writing-tests/attribute-rubric.md`
  (see "Reviewing a test's attributes" below). A benchmark test for a requirement that another
  suite already checks is a shim that returns that test's result (see "Reviewing a test for
  duplicates" below).
- `powershell/tests/` — **unit tests for the module itself**.

## Commands

- Unit tests: `./powershell/tests/pester.ps1` — run before pushing. These enforce
  naming, exports, help, and PSScriptAnalyzer conventions; fix what they flag.
- Build module: `./build/Build-MaesterModule.ps1`; validate: `./build/Test-MaesterModuleOutput.ps1`
- Website: `cd website && npm ci && npm start` · Report: `cd report && npm ci && npm run build`

## Hard rules

- Generated content — regenerate, never hand-edit: `website/src/data/versions.json`, `website/versioned_docs/` (the frozen 2.x docs), everything under
  `powershell/internal/generated/`, and the native `tests/eidsca/Test.EIDSCA.*` and
  `tests/orca/Test.ORCA.*` files the generators in `build/eidsca/` and `build/orca/`
  write. Edit the PowerShell source, comment-based help or generator templates and let
  automation regenerate. `powershell/assets/ConsoleContributors.json` (the dashboard's
  Featured contributor list) is written by `./build/Update-ConsoleContributors.ps1` from
  the website's contributor data.
- Never commit the website data that each build generates: the command pages in `website/docs/commands/`
  (everything but `readme.mdx`), `website/src/data/test-catalog.json`, `contributors.json` and `sponsors.json`.
  They are ignored by git. `website/scripts/prepare-data.mjs` writes them from the module source, the git
  history and GitHub before `npm run dev` and `npm run build`; `npm run refresh-data` writes them again.
  The build-website workflow builds and deploys maester.dev from main, so a merge needs no follow-up PR.
- A test is mapped to a framework in one place: the `Control` attribute, `<framework-key>:<requirement-id>`. A
  CIS test carries `Control = 'cis-m365:5.1.5.1'`, a CISA test `Control = 'cisa-scuba:MS.AAD.3.1'`, and any other
  test may name the same requirements. An ASD test carries `Control = 'essential-eight:ISM-1504'` (or `ism:<id>` for a
  control outside the maturity model). Every test in `tests/cis`, `tests/cisa` and `tests/asd` must name a requirement of its
  suite's framework. The engine builds `Benchmark` from the first `Control` that a framework file knows and adds
  that requirement's `Related` references to `Control`; do not repeat those, and do not add benchmark tags.
- A framework file is a catalogue, not a list of tests: `tests/<suite>/frameworks/<key>.json`
  (`tests/cis/frameworks/cis-m365.json`, `tests/cis/frameworks/cis-github.json`,
  `tests/cisa/frameworks/cisa-scuba.json`, and the generated `tests/asd/frameworks/essential-eight.json` and
  `tests/asd/frameworks/ism.json`, written by `build/asd/Update-AsdFramework.ps1` from the ISM OSCAL release),
  declared in the suite's `suite.json` (`Frameworks`: `Key`,
  `Version`). It holds the framework's name and version and each requirement's `Id` and facts (CIS `Level` and
  `Profile`; CISA `Criticality`, `Upstream` and `Related` NIST references; Essential Eight `Level` and `Strategy`;
  ISM `Guideline`, `Section` and `Applicability`), never the text of a benchmark and
  never a `Tests` list. When a new test implements a requirement the file does not have, add the requirement in
  the same commit, or `./build/Build-MaesterModule.ps1` and the unit tests fail.
- Checks read through the session cache. A run reports on one snapshot of the tenant, so no check, pack or helper
  passes `-DisableCache` or otherwise bypasses the Graph or GitHub cache, even to read data that changed during the
  session. Only the transport helpers listed in `powershell/tests/general/GraphCacheUsage.Tests.ps1` may offer the
  switch, and that test fails on any other use. Don't apply a review suggestion to bypass the cache.

## Repository layout — where files go

Full rules and reasoning: `website/docs/contributing.md` ("Repository layout"), published at
https://maester.dev/docs/contributing#repository-layout. `powershell/tests/general/RepositoryLayout.Tests.ps1`
enforces them. When writing or reviewing a change, check every added, moved or renamed file:

- Folder names under `tests/`, `powershell/` and `build/` are lowercase kebab-case
  (`global-secure-access`, not `GlobalSecureAccess`). No two paths may differ only in case.
- One name per service, the same everywhere: `ad`, `azure`, `azure-devops`, `copilot`,
  `copilot-studio`, `defender`, `entra`, `exchange`, `fabric`, `foundry`, `github`,
  `global-secure-access`, `graph`, `intune`, `purview`, `sharepoint`, `teams`, `xspm`.
  Folders name the product whose settings a check reads, never a theme: an AI check goes in
  the folder of its product (an Entra agent identity check in `entra/`) and declares
  `Area = 'ai'`. A new service must be added to the guide and the test.
- `tests/<suite>/` holds only `Test.<ID>.ps1`, `Test.<ID>.md`, `suite.json` and `README.md`, plus the suite's
  framework files, `frameworks/<key>.json` beside its `suite.json` (lowercase key; nothing else goes in a
  `frameworks/` folder).
  Suites: `maester/<service>/` (plus `drift/`; `maester/xspm/` has its own suite.json),
  `cis/`, `cisa/<service>/`, `asd/<service>/`, `ad/<area>/`, generated `eidsca/` and `orca/`, and `custom/`
  (reserved for users; never commit tests there).
- `powershell/public/` (exported) is grouped by job: `run/`, `connect/`, `report/`, `app/`,
  `packs/`, `services/<service>/`. `powershell/internal/` uses `engine/`, `session/`, `connect/`,
  `report/`, `app/`, `packs/`, `services/<service>/`, `checks/<suite>/<service>/`, `generated/`,
  `utility/`. Nothing sits directly in `public/` or `internal/`.

Summary:
1. **Primary Request and Intent:**
   - **Earlier (done):**
     - Map Maester and ZTA tests onto the Zero Trust Workshop, with a view per pillar.
     - Prototypes A to G are in artifact https://claude.ai/artifact/7ndw5XizGymcqbMt4x2FrJ.
     - Flyover details panel; no workshop links.
     - Fix scrolling in G and implement G in Maester.
     - Bundle the workshop data in the pack.
   - **"how can i run this locally":** answered with the dev server and the full-run instructions.
   - **"why did you change the type of chart/canvas in the diagram view from what was shown in G":**
     - G used Cytoscape 3.28.1 with a preset layout. I swapped it for HTML/SVG without asking.
     - Reasons: report size (~430 KB), theming and accessibility, and the scroll fix.
   - **Latest:** "i don't like the custom diagrm. if thats the case then lets use the swimlane view in Option A as the default, view and the progress table as the second view." This is done.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**
   - **Report app:** React with Preact compat and Vite singlefile, a hash router, and `mt-` CSS classes.
   - **Plan data:** the ZTA pack attaches the JSON `zero-trust-workshop` (schema `maester.zero-trust-workshop/1`).
   - **Task status:** done, partial, notdone, unknown, or manual.
   - **Flyover:** `mt-zt-fly`, z-index 39. The test sheet opens on top with `openTest`.
   - **Board (from Option A):**
     - Rows are swimlanes; columns are the phases First, Then, Next.
     - Cards carry a status-coloured left border; manual tasks have a dashed border.
     - Phase headers are sticky at `top: 57px`.
     - `@container (max-width: 720px)` stacks the phases under each lane.
   - **Filters:** non-matching tasks are hidden on the board.

3. **Files and Code Sections** (worktree `/Users/merill/github/maester/.claude/worktrees/zero-trust-view`, all uncommitted):
   - **New `report/src/components/report/ZeroTrustBoard.tsx`:**
     - Exports `ZeroTrustBoard({plan, area, current, selected, match, onSelect})` and `TaskIcon` (moved here from the deleted diagram file).
     - Renders a legend (done, partial, notdone, unknown, manual) and a `.mt-zt-board` with `role=table`.
     - The header row has the "Swimlane" column and the phase headers, each with a "You are here" pill and "x of y done".
     - Each lane row has a lane cell, then three `.cell` elements (each with `.phl` and the class `cur`/`none` as it applies) holding `Card` buttons.
     - Each card has id `mt-zt-card-<id>`, class `mt-zt-card s-<st>`, and shows the icon, the name, a Maester chip, and a sub line: "N of M checks pass", "Review yourself" or "Couldn't check", plus priority and "after X +n".
   - **Deleted:** `report/src/components/report/ZeroTrustDiagram.tsx` and `report/src/lib/zeroTrustLayout.ts`.
   - **`report/src/pages/report/ZeroTrustPage.tsx` edits:**
     - Imports `TaskIcon, ZeroTrustBoard` from `ZeroTrustBoard`, with `type View = "board" | "table"`.
     - The route reads `mode === "table" ? "table" : "board"`. `setView` navigates to `/zero-trust/${id}${v==="table"?"/table":""}`.
     - `area` defaults to `pillar.next[0]?.areaId`. The `focus`, `wide` and `cover` state was removed.
     - `reveal(t, view, smooth)` retries with requestAnimationFrame up to 20 times until `mt-zt-row-<id>` or `mt-zt-card-<id>` exists, then calls `scrollIntoView` with `block: center`.
     - `open()` clears the filters if the task doesn't match. On the board it sets the area; in the table it expands the task's groups. It reveals the task when opened from the list or a link.
     - `swap()` toggles the view, sets the area when going to the board, and reveals the task.
     - The toolbar segment is now "Swimlanes" (default) and "Table".
     - The panel button reads "Show in the swimlanes" or "Show in the table".
     - The table's area row has a "Swimlanes" link, which sets the area, switches to the board and scrolls to the top.
     - When no task in the area matches, the board shows "No task in X matches. Clear filters".
     - The header comment was updated.
   - **`report/src/styles/report.css`:**
     - Removed the diagram CSS (`.mt-zt-diagram`, stage, canvas, band, lane, edges, node, ghost, tools) and the `--zt-band` variables.
     - Added the `.mt-zt-boardwrap` (`container-type: inline-size`), `.mt-zt-legend`, `.mt-zt-board` grid (`minmax(130px,190px) repeat(3,minmax(0,1fr))`), `.mt-zt-brow` (`display: contents`), `.ph` sticky, `.ph.cur`, `.lane`, `.cell` (`.cur` tint) and `.mt-zt-card` styles, the phone padding media query, and the container query that stacks the board.
     - Updated the comments to name ZeroTrustBoard and "Swimlane board".
   - **`website/docs/packs/zero-trust-assessment.md`:** added a paragraph to the "Zero Trust plan" section describing the Swimlanes view (the default) and the Table view, and that selecting a task opens a panel on the right.
   - **Other uncommitted work from earlier is unchanged:**
     - The generator `build/zero-trust-workshop/`.
     - The workshop JSON in `packs/zero-trust-assessment/workshop/`.
     - The pack helpers.
     - `Add-MtReportAttachment -ContentType`.
     - JSON attachment redaction in `Get-MtHtmlReport`.
     - `zeroTrust.ts`, `sampleZeroTrust.ts`, `reportAttachments.ts`, `sampleExtras.ts`, `vite.config.ts`, `App.tsx`, `views.ts`.
     - Tests and docs.

   - **Card text overflowed at narrow widths.** Switched the stacking to a container query at 720 px and added `overflow-wrap: anywhere` to the card names.

   - **ESLint** found no config, so lint was skipped. `tsc -b` passes.

# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe's **Jev**, the first public **System One model**, answers typed questions about state your
application supplies. State is the text, images, and application data your code sends with a
request. Jev can answer a Choice among options, a Noul (the probability that a statement is true), a
Score on levels you describe, or a Box that locates something in an image. Each answer comes back as
typed data with calibrated probabilities, for your code to use.

The rest of this skill is guidance: patterns that tend to produce reliable integrations. None of it
is absolute. Models change, applications differ, and edge cases exist. When a situation calls for
something else, test the alternative and use your judgment.

## Judgments from Jev, decisions in code

Integrations tend to work best when Jev makes the judgments and code decides what to do with
them. Think of each decision as a **truth table**. Jev supplies the inputs, such as "Does the
customer sound frustrated?" or "Which product is the message about?". Code holds the logic that
maps those inputs to an action.

A question that asks Jev to make the decision, such as "Should this ticket be escalated?" or "What
should the agent do next?", usually means the question is at the wrong layer. Instead, break the
decision into the judgments it depends on, and write the decision itself in code, where it's
visible and testable. Writing out the table often shows gaps in the business logic too. A
combination of judgments with no defined outcome is a design question about the system, and it is
best settled in code.

## Live docs

The live docs are the source of truth for request syntax, SDKs, question types, limits, and current
model behavior. Read the relevant pages as part of the task.

- Start at the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt). Append `.md` to a page
  path to get the page as Markdown, and resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Exact request and response schemas: the [OpenAPI spec](https://api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json) and
  the [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/api.md) page. For an SDK, see the
  [Python](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/python-sdk.md) or
  [JavaScript](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/js-sdk.md) page and the types in the installed package.
- Question types: [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/primitives.md) and each type's own page,
  [structured instructions and criteria](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/advanced.md), and
  [images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/images.md).
- Models, context limits, and rate limits: [models](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/models.md). Known
  model weak spots and their workarounds are on the
  [jaggedness page](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/jaggedness.md).
- Architecture: [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/how-to-build.md),
  [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/patterns.md), and
  [cookbooks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md). The cookbook closest to your use case is a
  good starting point for a new workflow.

If you can't reach the live docs, use the installed SDK's types or local docs, and tell the user
you did. Leave out details that depend on the version rather than guessing them.

## Workflow

1. **Start from the decision logic.** Begin with what the application will show, select, change,
   or hand off. Sketch the truth table or rules that decide it, and list the inputs they need.
   Inputs that need an understanding of language or images make good questions. Arithmetic, dates,
   exact lookups, and policy usually belong in code. Aim for every question to feed the table, and
   give every combination of answers an outcome, including the case where a Noul lands between your
   thresholds. If code alone can already make the decision reliably, tell the user.
2. **Keep all question wording in one place.** Questions, options, criteria, and thresholds are the
   parts of an integration people audit and edit most. Keeping them together in one module makes
   that easier. [Design the state](#design-the-state) and
   [Write the questions](#write-the-questions) describe what tends to work.
3. **Probe the live API**: send test requests as described in
   [Test with the live API](#test-with-the-live-api). Use representative cases, hard cases, and
   negative cases. Keep going until the application behaves as intended.
4. **Integrate.** A few habits help here. Expose or log the exact request payload. When a call to
   the API fails, surface it as an error, not as an answer; for example, don't treat a failed call
   as a "no". Keep API keys on the server.

If the user's request is open-ended, offer the few directions from [Cookbooks](#cookbooks) that
best serve their goal, and recommend one. If the request is concrete, build it.

## Design the state

A useful check for any question is the **human test**: could a smart person, shown only this state
and this question, answer quickly by intuition? When a question fails the test, the fix is usually
in the state, not in the wording.

- **Give what a person would look at.** That means who sent each message, the full thread rather
  than a truncated last line, names rather than raw IDs or @-mention markup, and the item the
  question is about rather than the whole catalogue. State facts your code already knows, such as
  "all messages in `replies` were sent after the refund was issued", rather than leaving the model
  to work them out again.
- **Supply facts the model may lack**, such as what an internal product name or codename refers
  to.
- **Ensure every field in the state is relevant.** Irrelevant detail clutters the context and
  reduces accuracy. A field added for one question can sway the answer to another, and the model
  can read an empty list as a signal.
- **Be mindful when truncating.** Truncate long strings only when you need to, and check that the
  cut doesn't remove context the questions need.
- **Structure with named fields.** JSON objects with descriptive keys work better than a string of
  serialized JSON. They also let a question refer to each part by its path. Stable names such as
  `candidates.refund_policy` are easier to refer to than array positions.
- **Consider leaving out what no person could judge**, such as an unreadable crop or a distinction
  experts dispute. The model's answer there tends to be noise, and code will treat that noise as
  signal.

## Write the questions

Break complex judgments or decisions into their parts, and combine the answers in code with
weighted sums, boolean logic, thresholds, or other heuristics to reach the final decision. For
example, rather than asking "Is this fraud?" or "Is this spam?", ask the set of atomic questions
about what might make something fraud or spam. Each question tends to work best when it asks for
**one judgment** that a person could make at a glance.

- **Ask the concrete, observable thing.** Aim for something a person could point to: "Is a SQL
  query built by string concatenation here?" rather than "Are there SQL injection risks?".
- **One judgment per question; beware the "or".** Two conditions joined by "or" or "and" usually
  work better as two questions. Likewise, a list of rules usually works better as one question per
  rule.
- **Anchor intent to the goal.** When the judgment is about what someone wants, it helps to name
  their goal: "Which of these files does the user want copied?" rather than "Which of these names
  the main input?".
- **Name the subject directly.** "Where is the coffee mug in `photo`?" reads better than "Where is
  `target` in `photo`?" with the target defined somewhere else. Context that only one question
  needs, including an image, usually fits best in that question's instructions (the question text)
  or its criteria (the descriptions of its options, its levels, or what yes and no mean). Context
  that many questions share can go in the state once, and each question can refer to it by its
  exact path in backticks. When you ask the same question about many items, it usually works better
  to put each item into its own question than to give an ID the model has to look up in a shared
  list.
- **Each question is answered on its own.** Questions in a request can't see each other or each
  other's answers. Any context a question relies on belongs in the state or in that question.
- **Write plainly.** A question isn't an LLM prompt. Preambles, "consider X, Y, and Z" lists, and
  output-format instructions add noise. Descriptions of the options belong in the criteria, not in
  the question. Phrase the question so that a true answer means yes. Watch for double negatives,
  and for presuppositions such as "the next step".
- **Name the case that causes confusion.** If answers keep mixing up two outcomes, say in the
  criteria what separates them, using the specific case. For example, for "Is this a refund
  request?", note that a question about the refund policy is not a request. A vague exclusion such
  as "not other kinds of message" helps less, and can draw attention to the wrong answer.

### Criteria

- **Ask about the null case separately.** A Box always returns a location and a Choice always picks
  an option, even when nothing fits. Pair either one with a Noul in the same request that asks
  whether anything fits ("Is there a coffee mug in `photo`?", "Does `message` name any of our
  products?"), so code can tell when nothing does. As of Jev 1.14, this companion Noul usually works
  better than a "none of the above" option.
- **Option names are sent to the model; question IDs are not.** Names that describe the content
  (`refund_request`, `shipping_delay`) help the model. Positional names (`A`, `left`, `option_1`)
  give it nothing meaningful to go on and can bias the answer.
- **Keep options distinct and concrete.** Wording that options share with each other, or with the
  input, can pull probability toward those options. An option that covers several meanings is
  often worth splitting, because its probability can't tell code which meaning applied. Direction
  and magnitude usually work better as separate questions, so that the answer to one doesn't get
  mixed into the other.
- **Describe each Score level as a situation.** Each level should make sense when read on its own:
  "The customer mentions a minor inconvenience" rather than "More upset than the previous level".
- **Describe a Noul's `false` criterion as a concrete situation**, such as "the package arrived on
  time", rather than as "not late".
- **Use a Noul per statement when more than one can be true.** A Choice picks one option, so a
  message that is both a refund request and a complaint forces it to split probability between the
  two. Separate Nouls let each one be true on its own.

## Compose requests

**Bundle questions that share state.** A handy heuristic: if two calls would send the same state
with different questions, they can likely be one call. Questions are cheap and run in parallel, and
the state is read and paid for once. See
[parallel questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/parallel_questions.md).

**Ask speculatively**, meaning ask a question before you know whether you'll need its answer. A
question that only matters in some cases can go in the same request as the question that
identifies the case. Ask "Is `order` a return request?" and "Which item in `order.items` is being
returned?" together, and have code read the second answer only when the first is yes. The second
question doesn't need an "if" clause, because code handles the condition. See
[speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).

A second request is usually worth it when:

- code needs an answer to build the next state, fetch evidence, or choose the next options;
- a state field needed for one question measurably misleads another;
- different sets of questions need to be cached or versioned separately.

## Read the answers

### Confidence is rarely the gate

Naive implementations often use an answer's `confidence` as the check that decides whether code
acts. Confidence measures how concentrated an answer's probability distribution is, which is not
the same as how likely the answer is to be correct. Think about what the probabilities should look
like in your use case; another calculation over them may suit it better.

### Probabilities and thresholds

- **A probability is the likelihood that an answer is correct.** Jev isn't a calculator for
  probability problems. Ask it for judgments, and do any math on odds or probabilities in code. A
  Noul near 0.5 usually means the state doesn't settle the question.
- **The top answer is a good default**: the Choice's top option, or the Score's position.
- **0.7 and 0.3 make good starting thresholds for a Noul**: above 0.7 reads as yes, below 0.3 as no,
  and the band between means the question isn't settled, which can get its own row in the truth
  table. Adjust them when the application calls for it, and be wary of over-fitting them to a
  handful of test cases.
- **Look at Score distributions.** The Score's position can get pulled toward the middle and hide
  two-peaked answers, so look at the level probabilities before deciding which value your code
  reads.

## Test with the live API

Sending test requests to the live API is a great way to test questions against your data. Ask the
user for permission first. Get a budget for experimentation (TypeSafe is very inexpensive, so a
little can go a very long way), disclose what data will be sent (point out any personal or private
data), and say that their `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` will be used.

- Start with a few representative cases, plus hard ones and some whose answer is "no" or "nothing
  fits".
- Compare wordings by sending each variant as a separate question in one request, over the same
  state.
- Read individual answers, not only aggregates.
- Keep the exact request payload for each case so any result can be rerun.
- Check each change against cases you didn't use while tuning.

Make sure any agent that sends test requests has network access to the API endpoint.

### When an answer looks wrong

Check these, in this order:

1. the payload as actually sent;
2. the state, against the human test;
3. the options and candidates: is the right answer among them?
4. the scope of the questions: can each one be broken down into smaller judgments?
5. the wording.

If a clear question with complete state still gets an answer you're confident is wrong, check the
jaggedness page for the model you're using. It lists known weak spots and how to work around them.
If the behavior isn't listed, the TypeSafe team welcomes examples through the channel linked on
that page. In the meantime, work out an alternative approach with the user that avoids the weak
spot.

### Yellow flags

Typically, a good change is one that makes the definition clearer or improves the state. Check each
change on cases you didn't tune on. Wording written to produce a particular value is **prompt
gymnastics**, and it tends to break on new inputs and on the next model version. Some yellow flags:

- criteria that name specific test items, or that gain a clause for each failing case;
- caveats that explain away a model quirk;
- thresholds fitted to particular cases;
- tests that assert an exact probability;
- code that quietly overrides answers.

The structural fix is usually better state, a separate question, or code.

## Cookbooks

Each of these starting points combines questions to serve one goal. Ideas outside this list are
welcome.

- **Route and fill arguments.** One request identifies what the user is asking for and which
  values go in each argument. Code then calls the handler. See
  [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md) and
  [intent routing](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/intent-routing.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Code finds candidate values or spans of text, the model picks
  the intended one, and code copies or normalizes it. See
  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md),
  [date extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/date_extraction_cookbook.md), and
  [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates and ask how relevant each one is. See
  [line-by-line search](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/semantic_find.md),
  [re-ranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md), and
  [classifying RAG passages](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/classifying_rag_passages.md).
- **Turn answers into data.** Score each dimension once, then let code or users change the weights
  and views. If you have labeled outcomes, the answers can become features for a model. See
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check claims or fields against their evidence, and send the cases that
  fail to a person or a reasoning model. See
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).

The TypeSafe team is constantly adding cookbooks of well-tested patterns to the live documentation.
It's a good idea to check the [cookbooks index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md) for one
that fits the problem you're solving.

- **A probability is the likelihood that an answer is correct.** Jev isn't a calculator for
  probability problems. Ask it for judgments, and do any math on odds or probabilities in code. A
  Noul near 0.5 usually means the state doesn't settle the question.
- **The top answer is a good default**: the Choice's top option, or the Score's position.
- **0.7 and 0.3 make good starting thresholds for a Noul**: above 0.7 reads as yes, below 0.3 as no,
  and the band between means the question isn't settled, which can get its own row in the truth
  table. Adjust them when the application calls for it, and be wary of over-fitting them to a
  handful of test cases.
- **Look at Score distributions.** The Score's position can get pulled toward the middle and hide
  two-peaked answers, so look at the level probabilities before deciding which value your code
  reads.

## Test with the live API

Sending test requests to the live API is a great way to test questions against your data. Ask the
user for permission first. Get a budget for experimentation (TypeSafe is very inexpensive, so a
little can go a very long way), disclose what data will be sent (point out any personal or private
data), and say that their `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` will be used.

- Start with a few representative cases, plus hard ones and some whose answer is "no" or "nothing
  fits".
- Compare wordings by sending each variant as a separate question in one request, over the same
  state.
- Read individual answers, not only aggregates.
- Keep the exact request payload for each case so any result can be rerun.
- Check each change against cases you didn't use while tuning.

Make sure any agent that sends test requests has network access to the API endpoint.

### When an answer looks wrong

Check these, in this order:

1. the payload as actually sent;
2. the state, against the human test;
3. the options and candidates: is the right answer among them?
4. the scope of the questions: can each one be broken down into smaller judgments?
5. the wording.

If a clear question with complete state still gets an answer you're confident is wrong, check the
jaggedness page for the model you're using. It lists known weak spots and how to work around them.
If the behavior isn't listed, the TypeSafe team welcomes examples through the channel linked on
that page. In the meantime, work out an alternative approach with the user that avoids the weak
spot.

### Yellow flags

Typically, a good change is one that makes the definition clearer or improves the state. Check each
change on cases you didn't tune on. Wording written to produce a particular value is **prompt
gymnastics**, and it tends to break on new inputs and on the next model version. Some yellow flags:

- criteria that name specific test items, or that gain a clause for each failing case;
- caveats that explain away a model quirk;
- thresholds fitted to particular cases;
- tests that assert an exact probability;
- code that quietly overrides answers.

The structural fix is usually better state, a separate question, or code.

## Cookbooks

Each of these starting points combines questions to serve one goal. Ideas outside this list are
welcome.

- **Route and fill arguments.** One request identifies what the user is asking for and which
  values go in each argument. Code then calls the handler. See
  [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md) and
  [intent routing](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/intent-routing.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Code finds candidate values or spans of text, the model picks
  the intended one, and code copies or normalizes it. See
  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md),
  [date extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/date_extraction_cookbook.md), and
  [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates and ask how relevant each one is. See
  [line-by-line search](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/semantic_find.md),
  [re-ranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md), and
  [classifying RAG passages](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/classifying_rag_passages.md).
- **Turn answers into data.** Score each dimension once, then let code or users change the weights
  and views. If you have labeled outcomes, the answers can become features for a model. See
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check claims or fields against their evidence, and send the cases that
  fail to a person or a reasoning model. See
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).

The TypeSafe team is constantly adding cookbooks of well-tested patterns to the live documentation.
It's a good idea to check the [cookbooks index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md) for one
that fits the problem you're solving.
